items.title: Home
items.text:
brigade

Mise-en-place, ready for service.

A Copier template that adds mise tooling and CI to an existing project.

lint · build · test · release · publish · deploy · operateon GitHub · GitLab · Gitea · Forgejo · your laptop

Documentation · Getting started · Recipes · Changelog

Alpha. brigade's questions, tasks and generated files can still change before 1.0.0. Read the release notes and Updating before you update.

brigade is a Copier template that adds mise tooling and CI to an existing project.

items.title: What it does
items.text:
• Pins the project's tools (linters, formatters, test runners) in .brigade/, as mise tools rather than project dependencies.
  • Defines the pipeline stages as mise tasks (mise run lint, mise run test), with the tools you pick.
  • Generates a CI that installs mise and runs those stages, for GitHub, GitLab or Gitea/Forgejo.
  • Keeps all of it up to date: mise run brigade:update applies the latest brigade release.

The same commands run on a laptop (Linux, macOS, Windows: see Platforms) and in CI.

items.title: What it does not do
items.text:
brigade sets up the kitchen; it does not cook your dish.

  • Create the project: use the ecosystem's own tool (uv init, ...), then apply brigade on top.
  • Write source code or package manifests. Tool settings are options of the mise tasks, or a file in .brigade/configs/ for tools that read one: see Tool configs.

items.title: The kitchen
items.text:
In a restaurant, the brigade is the kitchen team: each cook runs one station, the chef calls the orders, and nothing starts before the mise en place, everything prepared and in its place. mise is named after it; brigade staffs the kitchen:

In the kitchen In brigade Mise en place mise install: every tool pinned and ready before you start One station per cook One file per tool, .brigade/conf.d/<tool>-brigade.toml, with its tasks The service, course after course The stages: lint, build, test, release, publish, deploy, operate The chef calling the orders mise run <stage>: every station's task for that stage The pass, where each plate is checked CI, running the same stages on every pull request The house recipe The template, with your answers in .brigade/copier/data.yml Fresh deliveries mise run brigade:update: a new release, delivered by Renovate if you like The chef inspecting the stations brigade:lint: brigade's files are as delivered, nobody salted the sauce

Next: Getting started.

items.title: CI platforms
items.text:
The pass: every plate is checked before it leaves the kitchen.

brigade generates the CI files and mise run brigade:update keeps them up to date: do not edit them. Change the stages through your answers, or add your own files.

Jobs only install mise and call mise run <stage>, so CI and laptops run the same tools.

On every platform, lint, build and test run on pull requests (merge requests on GitLab), side by side; release runs on pushes to the default branch, publish on X.Y.Z tags and manual runs, deploy after publish (by itself or not: deploy_auto) and on manual runs, and operate on manual runs and on the operate_schedule answer (scheduled pipelines on GitLab).

items.title: GitHub (ci: github)
items.text:
File Role .github/workflows/<stage>.yml One workflow per stage, with one job that checks out the code and runs the stage's action: lint.yml, build.yml and test.yml on pull requests, release.yml on pushes to the default branch, publish.yml on X.Y.Z tags and manual runs (then, with deploy_auto, a job that starts the Deploy workflow on the tag), deploy.yml when started, operate.yml on manual runs and on the operate_schedule answer. .brigade/ci/github/actions/<stage>/action.yml The stage's steps: install mise and the tools, then mise run <stage> with the stage's environment (Releasaurus, Renovate). Secrets are passed as inputs: token (release), renovate-token (operate). .brigade/ci/github/actions/mise/action.yml Installs the pinned mise (mise-action) and the tools, with a cache. publish and deploy install them without a cache.

GitHub only reads workflows in .github/workflows/: everything else lives in .brigade/.

jactionlint (jactionlint:lint) checks the workflows and the actions, with its default rules: actions pinned by commit SHA (Renovate updates the SHA and its version comment), permissions:, timeout-minutes, concurrency: (pull request runs cancel the older ones, release, publish and deploy runs wait), and no cache restored in publish and deploy.

items.title: Stages
items.text: Each stage is one workflow with one job, on Linux, running its action, or one job per named job when you list them: see Named CI jobs. To remove a stage or change its commands, see Stages.

items.title: Your own jobs
items.text:
For anything else (several OSes, other triggers), add your own workflow file next to them, with another name: brigade never touches it.

# .github/workflows/tests-os.yml
on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.brigade/ci/github/actions/test

items.title: GitLab (ci: gitlab)
items.text:
File Role .gitlab-ci.yml Stages, and includes every .brigade/ci/gitlab/*.yml and .gitlab/ci/*.yml. GitLab only reads this file. .brigade/ci/gitlab/default.yml The mise image, the tool cache and mise install. .brigade/ci/gitlab/<stage>.yml One job per stage, running mise run <stage>: lint, build and test in merge request pipelines (needs: [], side by side), release on pushes to the default branch, deploy on X.Y.Z tags and "Run pipeline", operate in scheduled pipelines.

To add jobs, create your own file in .gitlab/ci/: it is included automatically, and GitLab merges included files.

# .gitlab/ci/extra.yml
extra:
  stage: test
  script:
    - mise run lint

gitlab-ci:lint checks these files against the GitLab CI schema.

items.title: Named CI jobs
items.text:
Each stage is one CI job running mise run <stage>, and mise runs the stage's tasks in parallel inside it. When a stage is long, split it with the jobs answer: each job gets its own CI job, in parallel on separate runners, and runs its commands in order.

# .brigade/copier/data.yml
jobs:
  test:
    - name: unit
      run:
        - "mise run pytest:test"
    - name: python
      run:
        - "mise run ctt:test -- -t .ctt/python"
    - name: go
      run:
        - "mise run typos:lint"
        - "mise run ctt:test -- -t .ctt/go"
  • The keys are stages (lint, build, test, release, publish, deploy, operate); a job has a name (letters, digits, ., _, -; unique in its stage) and a run list.
  • Each job becomes a hidden <stage>-<name> task in .brigade/stages.toml, which its CI job runs (mise run test-unit...); the check shows its name.
  • A last job, named after the stage, passes when they all pass: the check to require in branch protection (GitHub, Gitea). On GitLab, the stage's job runs them as a parallel:matrix (test: [test-unit]...).
  • Locally, mise run test runs every job's commands one after the other; mise run test-unit runs one CI job.
  • The jobs replace the stage's tools (and <stage>_commands): a tool missing from them does not run. Add a job or a command when you add a tool or a ctt variant.
  • A stage missing from jobs stays one job.
  • From brigade 0.21: <stage>_jobs is gone; move its commands to jobs (one job each, with a name).

items.title: Manual run
items.text: To deploy again, or without a release, use "Run workflow" on the Deploy workflow (GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo) on a tag or a branch, or "Run pipeline" on GitLab: only deploy runs, nothing is published. To publish again, "Run workflow" on the Publish workflow, or retry the publish job on GitLab. To run operate now, use "Run workflow" on the Operate workflow (GitHub, Gitea), or a pipeline schedule on GitLab.

items.title: Gitea (ci: gitea) and Forgejo (ci: forgejo)
items.text:
Same layout as GitHub: .gitea/workflows/<stage>.yml (.forgejo/workflows/ on Forgejo) and .brigade/ci/gitea/actions/, the same for both.

  • Forgejo forked Gitea and their APIs differ: on Forgejo, Releasaurus and Renovate use their forgejo forge and platform, and the release bot token is RELEASAURUS_FORGEJO_TOKEN. A Forgejo project on ci: gitea (before brigade had ci: forgejo) fails its release once a release PR is open: set ci: forgejo in .brigade/copier/data.yml, run mise run brigade:update, and rename the RELEASAURUS_GITEA_TOKEN secret to RELEASAURUS_FORGEJO_TOKEN.
  • Forgejo Actions sets FORGEJO_TOKEN in every job (the job's token): brigade's actions empty it for mise, whose forgejo: backend would send it to the forge a tool is released on (gitea.com for tea), which refuses it.
  • mise is installed with its install script: Forgejo resolves actions from its own mirror, which has actions/checkout but not mise-action, and act (local runs) refuses full URLs. The script checks the archive against a checksum file from the same server, so it trusts HTTPS only: jactionlint:lint ignores that one finding (unverified-download).

items.title: None (ci: none)
items.text: Only .miserc.toml and .brigade/ (without ci/) are generated.

items.title: Contributing
items.text: Back of house: something burned, a tool missing from the station, or a hand in the kitchen.

items.title: Issues
items.text:
Open an issue with one of the forms:

  • 🔥 Something burned: a task, a generated file or the CI does not work as documented. Give your brigade version (_commit in .brigade/copier/answers.yml), the command and its full output, and your .brigade/copier/data.yml: with it, the same project can be generated to reproduce the bug. Try mise run brigade:update first: it may already be fixed.
  • 🔪 New tool for the station: a tool for the catalog. It must install with mise and run on its own; tools already planned are listed in #138.
  • 🧑‍🍳 New recipe: any other idea. Start with the need, then the idea.

Search the existing issues first, and never paste a secret or token.

items.title: Development
items.text:
Working on brigade itself. Requires mise and a running Docker (the Docker, Ansible and publishing variants use it).

mise install
mise run lint
mise run build            # the documentation site, strict
mise run test
mise run zensical:serve   # preview the site

PRs are squash-merged with their title as commit message: the pull request template (.github/pull_request_template.md) lists what to check before opening one.

items.title: Repository
items.text:
• copier.yml includes .copier/settings.yml and .copier/questions/: common.yml, then one file per tool in tools/.
  • template/ holds the generated files.
  • ctt.toml lists the test variants.
  • docs/ and zensical.toml hold this site.

brigade is generated by brigade: .miserc.toml, .brigade/ and the .github/workflows/ files come from the latest release, with the answers in .brigade/copier/data.yml (taplo's file list, ctt:test clearing .ctt/ first, the Renovate config path), and the lint settings skipping template/ and .ctt/ in .brigade/configs/. mise run brigade:update updates them after a release. brigade's own settings (the .ctt/ env, the e2e:* tasks) live in mise.toml: brigade is tested with the tools it ships, except the end-to-end tests on local forges (tests/e2e/, see below).

items.title: Lint
items.text: mise run lint checks this repo: yamllint, jactionlint, zizmor (brigade's own workflows and actions), taplo, editorconfig-checker, gitleaks, typos, ruff and ty (the scripts), rumdl (Markdown), lychee (links, external ones included: it needs the network), ls-lint (names) and the Renovate config schema.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
mise run test runs ctt:test: ctt renders each ctt.toml variant into .ctt/, creates a real project there with the ecosystem's tool, then runs its stages. The variants do not replay their generated CI (act, gitlab-ci-local): it ran their stages a second time; the CI files are still linted (jactionlint, gitlab-ci). See #211 for running them again. ctt only sees files tracked by git: git add new template files before testing.

brigade's CI runs these tests on Linux only.

items.title: Local forges
items.text:
brigade runs end to end on a local forge with its runner (Docker Compose, local only): gitea, forgejo, gitlab, or github (a ci: github project on Gitea, whose runner runs GitHub Actions workflows). Three tasks, as Molecule's, each taking the forge, then the types (python, python-direct, node, bun, docker, java-maven, java-gradle, helm, ansible, app; all by default):

  • mise run e2e:converge <forge> [type...]: starts the forge and its runner when they are not up (and prints its URL and login), then for each type in turn (they share Nexus and the cluster): its preparation when not done (the registries and its deploy target emptied, its project, repository and secrets, the push; the repository is printed), what CI does from the pull request to the deploys (below), then the checks of what came out (the published release, the deploys on their target). It resumes at the first step not done: a failure fixed in the tests is run again from there;
  • mise run e2e:destroy <forge> [type...]: with types, forgets them (the next converge starts them over); without, also removes the forge and its data (its containers, network and volumes); images stay for the next run;
  • mise run e2e:test <forge> [type...]: the types started over, converge, then destroy, even when a test fails.

mise run e2e:test all [type...] runs every forge in turn (Gitea, github on the same server, Forgejo, GitLab), prints each one's result, then does the big cleanup, even when a test fails: brigade's clones and the projects, and everything Docker no longer uses, Docker-wide (docker system prune --all, then docker volume prune --all: stopped containers, unused images and volumes, named ones included; images are pulled again when needed).

To work on a failure: converge, look at the forge, fix the tests, converge again; a fix to brigade's files needs the type started over (destroy <forge> <type>, then converge); destroy <forge> at the end. The tasks run on this machine; each type (tests/e2e/projects.py; the Python one with both Releasaurus workflows, python: a release PR; python-direct: no PR) is:

  1. the project: brigade applied from this checkout at its latest tag, then its files, tests/fixtures/projects/<type>/ (its code, lockfiles and mise.toml, without brigade); or brigade at its HEAD (uncommitted changes included) when that release lacks one of the type's tools or answers (the branch adds them), or with E2E_FROM_HEAD=1 (every type: a changed tool, a quicker run), then step 4 is skipped;
  2. its settings (secrets, <cli>:setup and <cli>:check), then the push;
  3. a pull request: lint, build, test; merged;
  4. brigade:update to this checkout's HEAD, in a pull request whose CI passes; merged;
  5. the release PR, then the X.Y.Z tag (not on github: GitHub's API);
  6. the publish, to a local Nexus (tests/fixtures/compose.yml): Python, npm, Maven and image repositories, each logged in as Nexus' deploy user; then the deploy that publish starts on the tag (Gitea, Forgejo; GitLab: the tag's pipeline), and the environments deployed by hand (prod);
  7. the checks: the release in Nexus, and where the type deploys, per environment. helm: its charts on a k3s cluster next to the forge (tests/fixtures/compose.yml, profile cluster), each checked running in its namespace; app (not on GitLab: #208) too, its image published to Nexus and pulled by the cluster, checked to be the release's. ansible (not on GitLab: #139): a playbook over SSH to a server (profile ssh), with a vault-encrypted variable, each checked by the file it writes (environment, commit, the vault's value).

The test projects' files are linted with this repo (mise run lint): their Helm charts start with # yamllint disable-file (Go templates), so none of their templates may render empty (a comment alone is not a manifest) nor start with {{- (it joins the first line to the comment).

The release, the publish and the deploy run with the checkout's files: a fix to them is tested before it is released.

The checkout is the projects' _src_path, mounted at the same path in the jobs, uncommitted changes included. GitLab takes a few minutes to start; with Nexus and the jobs, it peaks at about 3.2 GB of RAM (Docker needs 4 GB). github acts on Gitea, the same server. Each type's state is in .forges/<forge>-<type>.json, its project in /tmp/brigade-forges/projects/, and its note in .forges/<forge>-<type>.md: its time, every step's result and time, the failed jobs' last log lines. e2e:test all ends with a table forge × type (passed, the first failed step, skipped; with the type's time) and the run's time, also written to .forges/summary.md; each run replaces the notes.

mise run build builds this site in strict mode, which fails on broken links. CI deploys it (pages:deploy, to the gh-pages branch) on each release tag and on a manual run of the Deploy workflow.

items.title: Versions and releases
items.text:
Pinned versions are updated by Renovate (.brigade/configs/renovate.json, generated with renovate_updates: [brigade, dependencies, template] and renovate_automerge: true in .brigade/copier/data.yml), run every day by the generated Operate workflow (mise run operate, operate_schedule):

  • template/'s pins in one PR, fix(deps): update template, major updates included: it triggers a release;
  • the tests' pins (the forges and their services in tests/fixtures/, the test projects, the root mise.toml) in one PR, test(deps): update tests, no release (renovate.json5, brigade's own settings): ctt does not use them, run the end-to-end tests on it before merging.

brigade's generated files get the new versions like any project, through a release and mise run brigade:update; its other pins (Copier and pytest in ctt.toml, README.md and .copier/settings.yml) are updated by hand.

It needs a RENOVATE_TOKEN secret: a fine-grained token on this repo with contents, pull requests, issues, workflows and commit statuses read/write.

Commits and PR titles follow Conventional Commits. On each push to main, the CI's release job runs Releasaurus (mise run release): it opens or updates the release PR, and once merged tags X.Y.Z and updates CHANGELOG.md; Copier uses these tags as template versions. releasaurus.toml makes a release on feat, fix, perf, revert and breaking changes only: other commits do not change the template.

It uses the RELEASAURUS_GITHUB_TOKEN secret, a fine-grained token on this repo with contents, issues and pull requests read/write: unlike the workflow token, its release PR runs the checks and its tag starts the Deploy workflow.

items.title: Custom tasks
items.text:
The chef's specials: your own tasks, next to the house menu.

mise reads the files listed in .miserc.toml: brigade's, in .brigade/, then your own mise.toml and mise.local.toml at the project root. Copier never touches them, so your tasks and tools survive brigade:update. A file elsewhere (such as .mise/conf.d/) is not read.

A task named <name>:<stage> joins that stage, because each stage runs *:<stage>:

# mise.toml
[tools]
hadolint = "2.15.1"

[tasks."hadolint:lint"]
description = "Check the Dockerfile with hadolint"
run = "hadolint Dockerfile"

[tasks."integration:test"]
description = "Run integration tests"
run = "uv run pytest tests/integration"

mise run lint and mise run test now include them, locally and in CI.

items.title: System packages
items.text:
Some tools need OS packages (a library, an SSH client...) that mise tools do not cover. Declare them in your mise.toml, then install them with mise bootstrap packages apply:

# mise.toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"apt:openssh-client" = "latest"  # Debian, Ubuntu
"brew:jq" = "latest"             # macOS

mise never installs them on its own, and an entry is skipped on an OS its package manager does not run on. They are installed for the whole machine (often with sudo), not for the project, and Renovate does not update them. brigade does not generate them: see #188.

items.title: Getting started
items.text:
Tie your apron: your first service starts here.

Requires mise and git.

items.title: Create the project, then apply brigade
items.text:
uv init my-project
uvx copier@9.19.1 copy gh:pa-decarvalho/brigade my-project
cd my-project
mise install
mise -C .brigade lock
mise tasks

Copier asks a few questions: your tools, whether to customize their versions and commands, CI platform, optional mirrors. copier copy uses the latest release; add --vcs-ref X.Y.Z to pick a version. mise install installs the tools, then mise -C .brigade lock writes their exact versions and checksums to .brigade/mise.lock (see Lockfile): commit it. If mise says the config files are not trusted, run mise trust once in the project.

items.title: Run the stages
items.text:
mise run lint
mise run test

items.title: Lint before each commit
items.text:
Select the prek tool (in tools, or tools in .brigade/copier/data.yml), then:

mise run prek:install

This writes a git hook in .git/hooks/ that runs the hooks of .brigade/configs/prek.yaml, yours: mise run lint to start with, and any hook of the pre-commit ecosystem you add (see prek).

items.title: Generated files
items.text:
.miserc.toml                # mise files to read: brigade's, then mise.toml
.brigade/
  copier/answers.yml        # your answers, written by Copier
  copier/data.yml           # your answers, to edit: brigade:update applies them
  configs/                  # tool configs (yamllint.yml, ruff.toml...)
  mise.toml                 # uv and brigade:update
  stages.toml               # the stages
  mirror.toml               # only with mirrors
  conf.d/<tool>-brigade.toml  # one per tool, and the CI file linter
  mise.lock, .mise/locks/   # tools' versions and checksums (mise lock)
  ci/<ci>/                  # CI steps: actions (GitHub, Gitea), jobs (GitLab)
<CI files>                  # workflows or .gitlab-ci.yml: see CI platforms

Your own tasks and tools go in mise.toml: see Custom tasks.

items.title: Mirrors
items.text:
Your own suppliers, for kitchens that cannot shop at the open market.

Behind a corporate network, optional questions point downloads at internal mirrors (e.g. Nexus). They are written to .brigade/mirror.toml; leave them empty to download from the internet.

Question Example Used for github_mirror https://nexus.example.com/repository/github/ Tools mise downloads from GitHub releases (mise url_replacements). pypi_index https://nexus.example.com/repository/pypi/simple Python tools installed by mise (pipx:), and uv / uvx in tasks (UV_DEFAULT_INDEX).

mise still reads release metadata from mise-versions.jdx.dev or api.github.com. Allow them, or see mise's URL replacements.

items.title: Questions
items.text:
Taking the order: what goes on the menu.

Answers are saved in .brigade/copier/data.yml, where you change them (see Changing answers), and in .brigade/copier/answers.yml, Copier's own copy (do not edit).

Question Values Default Effect presets python, go, terraform, ansible, shell, docker, lua, docs, copier-template, security, ci, maintenance (each answered as its tool list) none Pre-select their tools in tools: see Presets. tools tools of the catalog brigade, yamllint, gitleaks, typos One .brigade/conf.d/<tool>-brigade.toml each, with its tasks. Stages follow from the tools. <stage>_enabled yes / no yes Keeps the stage: its mise task and its CI job. See Stages. <stage>_commands list of commands empty Commands of the stage, run in order, locally and in CI. Empty runs all its tools. jobs stages to lists of {name, run} empty CI jobs per stage, in parallel, each running its commands in order (locally, all in order). Replaces the stage's tools and <stage>_commands. See Named CI jobs. environments list of {name, auto} empty Where the deploy stage deploys a release, in order: the auto ones once it is published, the others when started. Empty: one. See Environments. deploy_auto yes / no yes Without environments, with the publish and deploy stages: deploy by itself once each release is published, else only when started by hand. See deploy. operate_schedule cron expression, e.g. 0 5 * * 1 empty GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo: when the Operate workflow runs, besides manual runs. Empty: manual runs only. On GitLab, set a pipeline schedule instead. pages_dir folder site With the pages tool: the folder your build writes the site to (dist for Vite). uv_publish yes / no no With the uv tool: publish the package on each release (uv:publish, see publish). npm_publish yes / no no With the node tool: publish the package on each release (node:publish, see publish). bun_publish yes / no no With the bun tool: publish the package on each release (bun:publish, see publish). deno_publish yes / no no With the deno tool: publish the package to JSR on each release (deno:publish, see publish). maven_publish yes / no no With the maven tool: publish the artifacts on each release (maven:publish, see publish). gradle_publish yes / no no With the gradle tool: publish the artifacts on each release (gradle:publish, see publish). helm_publish yes / no no With the helm tool: push the charts on each release (helm:publish, see publish). helm_install yes / no no With the helm tool: install the charts on a cluster in the deploy stage (helm:deploy, see helm). cargo_publish yes / no no With the rust tool: publish the crate on each release (rust:publish, see publish). customize_tools yes / no no Asks a version, a config file and a command for each selected tool: see Tools. ci github, gitlab, gitea, forgejo, none github CI files and their linter: see CI platforms. github_mirror URL empty Mirror of https://github.com/: see Mirrors. pypi_index URL empty PyPI simple index: see Mirrors.

items.title: Changing answers
items.text:
Your answers are all in .brigade/copier/data.yml. Edit them there, then run mise run brigade:update:

# Your answers: edit them, then run mise run brigade:update.
build_commands:
  - "uv build"
ci: "gitlab"
customize_tools: true
ruff_version: "0.16.0"
tools:
  - "brigade"
  - "ruff"

brigade:update applies them, then writes all the answers back to this file, sorted, with JSON values (double quotes) and lists indented under their key:

  • New questions of a release show up with their default (Renovate's update PR included): change them there too.
  • A removed key comes back with its last value: set the value you want instead.
  • A key that is not a question (a typo), or a question not asked (tool versions need customize_tools: true), is dropped.
  • Your comments and formatting are not kept.

To add or remove tools, brigade:add and brigade:remove edit tools in data.yml, then run brigade:update:

mise run brigade:add ruff pytest
mise run brigade:remove hadolint

Both end with the project's tools, the ones you can remove; the catalog lists the ones you can add. A new tool's questions take their defaults. When the update fails (an unknown tool, one your ci refuses, other uncommitted changes), data.yml is put back as it was.

When data.yml is your only change, brigade:update applies it without a commit first: review and commit the edit and the update together. Your edits are kept if the update fails or is stopped; after a killed run, the next brigade:update puts them back first (they wait in .git/brigade-data.yml). With other uncommitted changes, Copier refuses to update: commit them first. Until you run brigade:update, brigade:lint fails: the answers are not applied yet.

items.title: Recipes
items.text:
Tested dishes: a whole project, from the first commit to its release.

Each recipe is a real project that brigade's tests build and run end to end (ctt.toml): pick the same tools to get the same kitchen.

items.title: Python package
items.text:
A library with its tests and docs, released by Releasaurus and published to PyPI (or another index) on each tag. Tested as the python-github variant.

uv init --lib my-package
uvx copier@9.19.1 copy gh:pa-decarvalho/brigade my-package

Tick the python and docs presets, then add the rest in tools. In .brigade/copier/data.yml:

ci: "github"
uv_publish: true
tools:
  - "brigade"
  - "yamllint"
  - "gitleaks"

items.text:
An application shipped as a Docker image: tested as code (pytest) and as an image (container-structure-test), pushed to a registry on each release, not published to PyPI. Tested as the python-docker-github variant, which pushes to a local registry in Docker.

uv init --package my-app
uvx copier@9.19.1 copy gh:pa-decarvalho/brigade my-app

In .brigade/copier/data.yml:

ci: "github"
tools:
  - "brigade"
  - "yamllint"

  - "zizmor"

Stage What runs lint brigade, YAML, spelling, .editorconfig, secrets, workflows (zizmor), Python (ruff, ty), vulnerable dependencies in uv.lock (osv-scanner), the Dockerfile (hadolint, checkov) build docker build . test pytest, the image's content (container-structure-test) release the release PR (it bumps pyproject.toml), then the tag (releasaurus) publish the image, tagged X.Y.Z and latest, pushed to ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo> (docker) operate dependency updates, uv.lock and the FROM image included (renovate)

No uv tool: it builds a package (uv build), which an app does not need; the Dockerfile installs the app. A Dockerfile from uv's image:

FROM ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.13.8-python3.14-trixie-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 UV_LINK_MODE=copy UV_NO_CACHE=1
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock README.md ./
COPY src ./src
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-dev

items.title: Tools
items.text:
The stations of the brigade, and who works at each one.

Pick your tools in one list when applying brigade. A tool brings its version and all its tasks, in one file: .brigade/conf.d/<tool>-brigade.toml, listed in .miserc.toml. Its tasks run at the project root.

Tasks are named <tool>:<action>. Stages run in this order: lint, build, test, release, publish, deploy, operate, and each runs every <tool>:<stage> task. Any other action, such as zensical:serve, stays out of the pipeline.

items.title: Stages
items.text:
For each stage, Copier asks whether to keep it, then its commands.

  • Answer no to remove the stage: no mise task, no CI job.
  • Leave the commands empty to run all the stage's tools. A stage without tools does nothing.
  • Give commands to run them instead, in order, locally and in CI:
lint_commands: ["mise run ruff:lint", "mise run typos:lint"]

items.title: Presets
items.text:
The presets question, asked before tools, pre-selects tools: tick or untick them in tools before going on. Only tools decides what the project gets; a preset changed in a later brigade release does not change existing projects. A preset's tools never change: its answer is checked against the choices on each brigade:update, so a new list is a new preset. A preset's answer is its tool list, e.g. presets: [[ruff, ty, pytest, uv]] in .brigade/copier/data.yml.

Preset Tools python ruff, ty, pytest, uv go golangci-lint node node, biome (JavaScript or TypeScript) bun bun, biome (JavaScript or TypeScript with Bun) deno deno (JavaScript or TypeScript with Deno) rust rust java maven (Java with Maven) java-gradle gradle (Java with Gradle) terraform tflint, checkov, opentofu kubernetes helm ansible ansible-lint, molecule, ansible shell shellcheck, shfmt docker hadolint lua stylua docs rumdl, zensical, pages (GitHub, GitLab) copier-template ctt security osv-scanner, checkov, zizmor (GitHub) ci act (GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo) or gitlab-ci-local (GitLab): replays the CI maintenance renovate, releasaurus

items.title: Tool configs
items.text:
Tools that read a config file get one in .brigade/configs/, created when the tool is selected; removing the tool from tools removes it. Paths in it are relative to the project root.

  • brigade's settings (the folders to skip, such as .mise-data/ and .mise/): brigade-owned, like the rest of .brigade/. brigade:update updates them and brigade:lint fails when one is edited. For your own settings, write your own file (start from a copy of brigade's, or extend it where the tool allows: extend in ruff, import in cspell, extends in yamllint, biome and rumdl), and set <tool>_config to its path (see Customize); it then keeps your settings, and brigade's later changes are yours to follow.
  • Your content (goreleaser, container-structure-test, sqlfluff, prek: your builds, tests, SQL dialect, hooks): created once with a starting point, then yours: brigade:update keeps it, brigade:lint skips it.
Tool Config Owner Your usual config file, with brigade's yamllint .brigade/configs/yamllint.yml brigade's (yamllint_config) .yamllint: not read ruff .brigade/configs/ruff.toml brigade's (ruff_config) [tool.ruff] in pyproject.toml, ruff.toml: not read ty .brigade/configs/ty.toml brigade's (ty_config) [tool.ty] in pyproject.toml, ty.toml: not read typos .brigade/configs/typos.toml brigade's (typos_config) _typos.toml, typos.toml: still read, both apply taplo .brigade/configs/taplo.toml brigade's (taplo_config) taplo.toml: not read rumdl .brigade/configs/rumdl.toml brigade's (rumdl_config) .rumdl.toml: not read editorconfig-checker .brigade/configs/editorconfig-checker.json brigade's (editorconfig_checker_config) .editorconfig-checker.json: not read (.editorconfig still is) ansible-lint .brigade/configs/ansible-lint.yml brigade's (ansible_lint_config) .ansible-lint: not read vale .brigade/configs/vale.ini brigade's (vale_config) .vale.ini: not read codespell .brigade/configs/codespell.cfg brigade's (codespell_config) .codespellrc: not read biome .brigade/configs/biome-brigade.jsonc brigade's (biome_config) biome.json, biome.jsonc: not read trivy (releasaurus_config) releasaurus.toml: not read maven .brigade/configs/maven-settings.xml (with maven_publish) brigade's (maven_config) ~/.m2/settings.xml: still read, both apply gradle Other tools read their usual config file (.golangci.yml, .tflint.hcl, stylua.toml, lychee.toml, .markdownlint-cli2.yaml, .prettierrc, .clang-format...).

items.title: codeceptjs
items.text:
codeceptjs runs end-to-end tests: CodeceptJS drives Chromium through its Playwright helper, against your app. CodeceptJS and Playwright are your dev dependencies (npm install -D codeceptjs playwright, then npx codeceptjs init): the helper loads Playwright next to CodeceptJS, so mise cannot install them apart, and their versions are in your package.json. It needs the node tool, and waits for node:test, which also runs npm ci.

Your codecept.conf.* holds your tests, your app's URL, and the server they need: CI runs each stage in a fresh job, without the build stage's output, so start it in bootstrap (and stop it in teardown), e.g. a static server on your build, or ng serve. The task installs Chromium, and on Linux its system packages (with sudo outside CI). Add CodeceptJS's output folder (e.g. e2e/output/) to your .gitignore.

items.title: prek
items.text:
prek runs git hooks, for local use; it stays out of the pipeline, which CI runs anyway. prek is a faster, single-binary pre-commit: same config format, same hooks. Its config, .brigade/configs/prek.yaml, is yours: brigade creates it once, then never changes it. It starts with prek's builtin hooks, fast and offline, on the committed files:

  • check-merge-conflict: conflict markers, also those brigade:update leaves;
  • check-added-large-files: files over 500 KiB;
  • check-case-conflict, check-illegal-windows-names: names that break on macOS or Windows;
  • mixed-line-ending, trailing-whitespace, end-of-file-fixer: they fix the files and fail the commit; stage the fixes and commit again.

Then mise run lint, the lint stage as in CI. Add hooks from the pre-commit ecosystem there (they download their own tools), or repo: local hooks that call your mise tasks.

mise run prek:install writes the hook into .git/hooks/, each clone once, in place of any hook already there (--force): the hook of brigade 0.25 and earlier, or one you wrote, whose commands go in prek.yaml as repo: local hooks. The hook calls this prek by its install path, so run it again after a prek version change. mise run prek:run runs the hooks on every file. Skip them for one commit with git commit --no-verify.

items.title: Repository settings
items.text:
Each forge's CLI comes with a check, for local use (not a stage): gh:check (GitHub), glab:check (GitLab), tea:check (Gitea, Forgejo). It reads the repository's settings that the selected tools need, with your login (gh auth login, glab auth login, tea login add), changes nothing, and fails when a required one is missing, with where to change it:

Tool GitHub GitLab Gitea, Forgejo always squash merge only, the pull request title as the commit squash commits required squash merge only releasaurus RELEASAURUS_GITHUB_TOKEN, else Actions allowed to create pull requests RELEASAURUS_GITLAB_TOKEN RELEASAURUS_GITEA_TOKEN, RELEASAURUS_FORGEJO_TOKEN on Forgejo (advised) renovate RENOVATE_TOKEN; auto-merge allowed with renovate_automerge RENOVATE_TOKEN; RENOVATE_GITHUB_COM_TOKEN and an active pipeline schedule (advised) RENOVATE_TOKEN; RENOVATE_GITHUB_COM_TOKEN (advised) pages Pages published from gh-pages Pages enabled

Secrets and CI/CD variables are looked up in the repository and its organization or group. Only admins (maintainers on GitLab) can list them: for others, they show as unknown.

gh:setup, glab:setup and tea:setup change the missing settings that need no secret value (merge method, auto-merge, Actions allowed to create pull requests, Pages once the first deploy has pushed gh-pages), then report the others as the check does: set the secrets yourself, as printed. Run it once on a new repository, as an admin.

mise run brigade:update runs the check at the end, outside CI, as a notice that never fails the update: a new tool may need a new setting.

items.title: Platforms
items.text:
brigade's own files run on Linux, macOS and Windows; each tool runs where it is supported. CI runs on Linux, so these limits only matter for local runs (mise run <stage>, git hooks). Known limits on Windows:

  • taplo: fails on checkouts with CRLF line endings (git config core.autocrlf false, or * text eol=lf in .gitattributes).
  • ctt: ctt 3.0.0 fails inside a git repository.
  • rust: needs the MSVC build tools (Visual Studio Build Tools, C++ workload) to link.
  • ansible-lint, molecule, ansible: Ansible does not run on Windows (use WSL).
  • act, gitlab-ci-local, docker, container-structure-test: need Docker with Linux containers (Docker Desktop, WSL 2).

items.title: brigade
items.text:
brigade:lint renders the template at the version of .brigade/copier/answers.yml, with your answers, into a temporary folder, and compares it with your brigade-owned files (.miserc.toml, .brigade/, the generated workflows or .gitlab-ci.yml). An edited or deleted file fails the lint stage, locally, in the git hook and in CI: brigade:update would overwrite it. Run mise run brigade:update to restore them. An edited .brigade/copier/data.yml fails it too until brigade:update applies it (see Changing answers).

It also fails when git ignores a brigade-owned file, which would then be missing in CI: a .gitignore pattern such as build (written by gradle init) matches .brigade/ci/<ci>/actions/build/ too. Anchor it to the root: /build.

It also tells when a newer brigade release is out (copier check-update), without failing: run mise run brigade:update, or let Renovate open the PR.

It needs access to the template (gh:pa-decarvalho/brigade, through git) on each run. Offline, behind a proxy, or to edit a generated file on purpose, remove brigade from your tools.

items.title: release
items.text:
CI runs this stage on its own, on pushes to the default branch: lint, build and test already ran on the pull request.

With releasaurus, Releasaurus reads the Conventional Commits since the last tag and opens or updates a release pull request, with the next version and a CHANGELOG.md. Once you merge it, the next run tags X.Y.Z (no v) and publishes the release on your forge. It works on GitHub, GitLab, Gitea and Forgejo.

Its config, .brigade/configs/releasaurus.toml (brigade's, read from the default branch through the forge's API, so commit it):

  • Releases on feat, fix, perf, revert and breaking changes only: other commits (ci:, docs:, chore:...) are left out of the version and CHANGELOG.md.
  • Tags X.Y.Z, with no v.
  • Updates your manifests to the new version in the release pull request (release_type), from your tools: uv → pyproject.toml, node → package.json and package-lock.json, bun → package.json, rust → Cargo.toml and Cargo.lock, go → version.go, helm → Chart.yaml, maven → pom.xml, gradle → version = "X.Y.Z" in build.gradle(.kts) or version=X.Y.Z in gradle.properties. With none or several of them, none. releasaurus_release_type picks another (php, ruby...) or none (see Customize). uv.lock is not updated: uv rewrites it on the next uv lock or uv run.

Two workflows (releasaurus_workflow, see Customize):

  • pr (default): a release pull request to merge; the next run tags it.
  • direct: each push with a releasable commit is released at once, with no pull request (releasaurus release-direct): the version and CHANGELOG.md are committed to the default branch, then tagged. With the CI's own token, the tag starts no CI: on GitHub and Gitea, set the bot token below so that publish runs. When the default branch is protected, that token must be allowed to push to it (the CI's own token cannot be):
  • GitHub: add the token's owner to the bypass list (ruleset: "Repository admin"; classic branch protection: leave "Do not allow bypassing the above settings" off, for admins).
  • GitLab: "Allowed to push and merge" on the protected branch includes the token's role (Maintainers by default: a project token with the Maintainer role).
  • Gitea, Forgejo: add the token's user to the branch protection's push whitelist.

For your own settings (prereleases, a monorepo, changelog options), set releasaurus_config to your file, with tag_prefix = "" in its [[package]] to keep the tags brigade's CI publishes. See Releasaurus configuration.

On GitHub and Gitea, it works with the CI's own token, with three manual steps:

  • GitHub: allow the workflow token to open pull requests (Settings → Actions → General → "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests", off in new repositories), else the release fails with Failed to create pull request:
gh api -X PUT repos/<owner>/<repo>/actions/permissions/workflow \
  -f default_workflow_permissions=read -F can_approve_pull_request_reviews=true

  • The release pull request starts no checks (GitHub shows failed runs with no job): re-run them, or merge with a bypass of the required checks.

  • The tag starts no CI: run publish by hand after each release.

A bot token avoids all three: the pull request and the tag start the CI as usual. GitLab needs the token: until it is set, the first pipeline on the default branch fails (API authentication failed: Token not provided); once it is, retry the failed release job ("Run pipeline" only deploys). A project token, created and stored without being printed:

glab token create releasaurus --access-level maintainer --scope api \
  --scope write_repository --duration 365d --output text \
  | glab variable set RELEASAURUS_GITLAB_TOKEN --masked

Merge pull requests with squash, the title being the commit: GitLab's default merge commit can leave a branch's older commits out of the next release.

CI Secret or CI/CD variable (bot token) Scopes GitHub RELEASAURUS_GITHUB_TOKEN Contents, Issues and Pull requests: read and write GitLab RELEASAURUS_GITLAB_TOKEN api, write_repository Gitea RELEASAURUS_GITEA_TOKEN repository, issue and misc: read and write Forgejo RELEASAURUS_FORGEJO_TOKEN repository, issue and misc: read and write

items.title: publish
items.text:
CI runs this stage on tags X.Y.Z (or vX.Y.Z), such as the ones Releasaurus pushes, and on a manual run ("Run workflow" on the Publish workflow; GitLab: retry the job).

It publishes the tagged version as an artifact to a registry (uv, node, bun, deno, rust, maven, gradle, docker, goreleaser, helm): a package, an image or a chart, installed by whoever needs it. Publishing belongs here, not in release: release runs on every push to the default branch and only decides the version, while publish runs once per tag and is the only job that gets the registry tokens. A version is published once: registries refuse it again, so running publish again on the same tag fails or does nothing new (see each tool below). To install a release again, run deploy, which publishes nothing.

deno publish, cargo publish and GoReleaser refuse a tree with uncommitted changes. In CI, mise can rewrite .brigade/mise.lock (it records an npm tool's provenance when it installs it, which mise lock leaves out): when that file and .brigade/.mise/ are the only changes, deno:publish and rust:publish add --allow-dirty, and goreleaser:publish adds --skip=validate (which also skips GoReleaser's tag checks). Any other change still stops them.

goreleaser builds the Go binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows and attaches the archives and their checksums to the release Releasaurus made for the tag (it needs Go: the go tool). GitHub: with the workflow token. GitLab: add a GITLAB_TOKEN CI/CD variable (a token with the api scope); a self-managed GitLab also needs its URLs in the config (gitlab_urls). Add dist/ to your .gitignore. A manual run needs a tag at the checked out commit.

node:publish (the node tool, with the npm_publish: true answer) publishes the package with npm publish, once per tag: the version is the one in package.json, which Releasaurus bumps in the release PR. Build it in a prepublishOnly script (npm run build). In CI, add an NPM_TOKEN secret (CI/CD variable on GitLab), and give npm the line that reads it in your .npmrc: //registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=${NPM_TOKEN} (another registry: its host, and publishConfig.registry in package.json). A scoped public package needs "publishConfig": {"access": "public"}. A version already published fails: a manual run on the same tag does nothing new.

bun:publish (the bun tool, with the bun_publish: true answer) publishes the package with bun publish, as node:publish does: the version is the one in package.json, which Releasaurus bumps, the NPM_TOKEN secret is read by your .npmrc, and a version already published fails.

deno:publish (the deno tool, with the deno_publish: true answer) publishes the package to JSR with deno publish --set-version X.Y.Z: the version is the tag's (Releasaurus does not update deno.json). In CI, add a JSR_TOKEN secret (CI/CD variable on GitLab), a token of your JSR account. A version already published fails.

rust:publish (the rust tool, with the cargo_publish: true answer) publishes the crate with cargo publish, once per tag: the version is the one in Cargo.toml, which Releasaurus bumps in the release PR. In CI, add a CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN secret (CI/CD variable on GitLab): a crates.io API token with the publish-update scope (and publish-new for the first release). Another registry: publish = ["<name>"] in Cargo.toml and the registry in .cargo/config.toml; cargo reads its token from CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_TOKEN, which your mise.toml can take from the same secret ([env]: CARGO_REGISTRIES_<NAME>_TOKEN = "{{env.CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN}}"). A version already published fails: a manual run on the same tag does nothing new.

maven:publish (the maven tool, with the maven_publish: true answer) publishes the artifacts with mvn deploy, once per tag: the version is the one in pom.xml, which Releasaurus bumps in the release PR (a -SNAPSHOT version goes to a snapshot repository). The repository is MAVEN_REPOSITORY_URL (Nexus, Artifactory, GitLab or Gitea package registry...): set it in your mise.toml ([env]) or as a CI variable; else distributionManagement in your pom.xml, whose repository needs the id brigade for the login. In CI, add MAVEN_USERNAME and MAVEN_PASSWORD secrets (CI/CD variables on GitLab), read by .brigade/configs/maven-settings.xml (Maven's global settings: your ~/.m2/settings.xml still applies). A release repository refuses a version already published: a manual run on the same tag fails.

gradle:publish (the gradle tool, with the gradle_publish: true answer) runs gradle publish, once per tag: your build applies the maven-publish plugin with its publications, and its version is the one Releasaurus bumps in the release PR. With MAVEN_REPOSITORY_URL set (your mise.toml [env] or a CI variable), .brigade/configs/gradle-init.gradle (an init script) adds it as a repository named brigade, logged in with the MAVEN_USERNAME and MAVEN_PASSWORD secrets (CI/CD variables on GitLab), over plain HTTP for an http:// URL; else only the repositories of your build. A release repository refuses a version already published: a manual run on the same tag fails.

docker builds the image of the tag and pushes it as X.Y.Z and latest (.brigade/scripts/docker_publish.py). The image is DOCKER_IMAGE (registry/owner/name, in your mise.toml [env] or a CI variable), else the repository's: ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo> on GitHub, pushed with the workflow token (the job has packages: write), <server>/<owner>/<repo> on Gitea. Another registry, or Gitea: add DOCKER_USERNAME and DOCKER_PASSWORD secrets. It needs Docker in CI, which brigade's GitLab image does not have: docker and container-structure-test are not offered on GitLab yet. A manual run needs a tag at the checked out commit.

helm:publish (the helm tool, with the helm_publish: true answer) packages each chart at the tag's version (helm package --version X.Y.Z) and pushes it (.brigade/scripts/helm_charts.py). The registry is HELM_REGISTRY (oci://host/path, http://host/path for a plain HTTP one; in your mise.toml [env] or a CI variable), else the repository's: oci://ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo> on GitHub, pushed with the workflow token, <server>/<owner>/<repo> on Gitea. Another registry, or Gitea: add HELM_REGISTRY_USERNAME and HELM_REGISTRY_PASSWORD secrets (CI/CD variables on GitLab, where HELM_REGISTRY is needed). A manual run needs a tag at the checked out commit.

uv:publish (the uv tool, with the uv_publish: true answer) publishes the Python package built by uv (uv build --clear, then uv publish without the empty UV_PUBLISH_* variables, which GitHub and Gitea pass for a secret that is not set), once per tag: the version is the one in pyproject.toml, which Releasaurus bumps in the release PR. The index is PyPI, or the upload URL in UV_PUBLISH_URL (Nexus, Artifactory, GitLab or Gitea package registry...): set it in your mise.toml ([env]) or as a CI variable. In CI, add a UV_PUBLISH_TOKEN secret (CI/CD variable on GitLab): the index's token (on PyPI, an API token scoped to the project once it exists); or, for an index with a user and a password (Nexus...), UV_PUBLISH_USERNAME and UV_PUBLISH_PASSWORD. A manual run on a tag already published fails unless UV_PUBLISH_CHECK_URL is set to the index URL (https://pypi.org/simple/), which skips the files already there.

items.title: deploy
items.text:
It deploys the tagged version to an environment (pages, ansible, helm with helm_install: true). It publishes nothing, so it can run as often as needed.

CI runs it:

  • After publish, on the same tag: by itself with deploy_auto: true (the default), or only when you start it with deploy_auto: false. GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo: the Publish workflow's last job starts the Deploy workflow on the tag (.brigade/scripts/ci_dispatch.py, with the workflow token, which may start a workflow this way). GitLab: the deploy job of the tag's pipeline, run by itself or by hand ("Play").
  • By hand: "Run workflow" on the Deploy workflow, on a tag (that release again) or a branch (e.g. a typo in the documentation); GitLab: "Run pipeline" (deploy only), or retry the job in the tag's pipeline.

Without the publish stage (publish_enabled: false), it runs on X.Y.Z tags itself.

items.title: Environments
items.text:
The environments answer lists where the same release is deployed, in order, each automatic or not:

environments:
  - {name: dev, auto: true}
  - {name: qa}
  - {name: prod}

Once a release is published, the automatic ones are deployed; the others when you start them, on the release's tag. The release is published once: each environment gets the same version, with its own settings. Empty (the default): one deployment, automatic with deploy_auto.

The deploy tasks read the environment in BRIGADE_ENVIRONMENT. Locally: BRIGADE_ENVIRONMENT=qa mise run deploy.

Start one by hand Its secrets and variables GitHub "Run workflow" on the Deploy workflow, environments: ["qa"] (a JSON list: several at once); one job per environment an environment per name, holding them under their usual names (KUBECONFIG_DATA); its protection rules (required reviewers: public repositories or paid plans) apply Gitea, Forgejo the same no environment secrets: suffixed with the environment, KUBECONFIG_DATA_QA (pre-prod: _PRE_PROD), else the plain name for all GitLab one job per environment in the tag's pipeline (deploy-qa), automatic or "Play"; "Run pipeline" offers them all CI/CD variables scoped to the environment

A name not in the answer fails before deploying. pages publishes one site: on GitLab, from the first environment's job. The order (qa before prod) is yours, or the forge's protection rules'. Named deploy jobs (jobs) do not combine with environments yet.

items.title: helm
items.text:
helm:deploy (the helm tool, with helm_install: true) installs or upgrades each chart on a cluster, from the tag's checkout (the same chart helm:publish pushed): helm upgrade <folder> <chart> --install --rollback-on-failure, which waits until the release is ready and rolls it back when it is not (.brigade/scripts/helm_charts.py).

  • The cluster: the KUBECONFIG_DATA secret, a kubeconfig's content (written to a temporary file); else kubectl's usual config (locally).
  • The namespace: the HELM_NAMESPACE variable, else the environment's name, else the kubeconfig's; created when missing.
  • The values: the chart's values.yaml, plus values-<environment>.yaml next to it when it exists (values-prod.yaml).
  • A kubeconfig for CI: a service account with the rights to install the charts' resources in the namespace, and a token that does not expire. GitLab cannot mask a value on several lines: protect the variable instead (and the tags), or keep the cluster's credentials out of the repository's settings.

pages needs GitHub or GitLab, and a <tool>:build task that writes the site to the pages_dir folder (site by default): zensical, node (a Vite app: pages_dir: dist), or your own (for example mkdocs:build, see Custom tasks).

  • GitHub: the site is pushed to the gh-pages branch. In Settings → Pages, choose "Deploy from a branch" and gh-pages.
  • GitLab: the job publishes the pages_dir folder with pages.publish (GitLab 17.10 or later). The site is private by default, even in a public project: in Settings → General → Visibility, set Pages to "Everyone" (glab api -X PUT projects/:id -f pages_access_level=enabled).

The site's base path depends on the forge: GitHub serves https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/; GitLab serves it at the root of a unique domain, https://<project>-<hash>.gitlab.io/ (on by default; without it, https://<namespace>.gitlab.io/<project>/, whose certificate fails when the namespace has a dot). Set it in your build: Vite's base, Angular's baseHref, zensical's site_url. Your end-to-end tests serve the build under the same base, so they pass either way: check the deployed site once.

Add site/ and .cache/ to your .gitignore.

items.title: operate
items.text:
Operations that do not belong to a release, such as renovate:operate. Run it with mise run operate, or in CI:

  • GitHub, Gitea: "Run workflow" on the Operate workflow, and on the operate_schedule answer (a cron expression, e.g. 0 5 * * 1 for Mondays at 5:00 UTC).
  • GitLab: scheduled pipelines only (CI/CD → Schedules; "Play" runs one now), since "Run pipeline" deploys.

Renovate reads brigade's config, .brigade/configs/renovate.json (RENOVATE_CONFIG_FILE): no renovate.json is needed, so there is no onboarding PR. What it updates is the renovate_updates answer, a list:

  • brigade (the default): brigade's updates, see brigade updates;
  • dependencies: your project's own (package.json, pyproject.toml, your workflows...), with Renovate's config:recommended;
  • template: the pins of a Copier template's template/ folder made like brigade's (brigade's own repository), in one fix: PR.

Your own Renovate config (renovate.json, .github/renovate.json5...) adds to it and wins, e.g. "automerge": true; without dependencies, "enabledManagers": [] there also updates your dependencies. To replace it all, point renovate_config to your own file (keep brigade's customManagers and packageRules entries for brigade's updates).

For Renovate, CI sets the platform, the endpoint and the repository; add a RENOVATE_TOKEN secret (CI/CD variable on GitLab). On GitHub, the job commits as the token's owner, with their noreply address (RENOVATE_GIT_AUTHOR); elsewhere, set gitAuthor in your Renovate config if needed. See Renovate's token permissions.

Off GitHub, also add a RENOVATE_GITHUB_COM_TOKEN secret (CI/CD variable on GitLab): many dependencies live on github.com (mise's github: and aqua: tools, github-releases, npm packages' repositories), whose API without a token soon hits its rate limit, so Renovate skips some lookups and opens PRs without release notes. Any github.com token works, with no permissions: a fine-grained token with "Public repositories" access. See Renovate's github.com token.

items.title: brigade updates
items.text:
renovate:operate also follows brigade: on a new release, it opens a PR that runs mise run brigade:update to that version, on every CI platform, as a ci(deps): commit (no release). Copier shows conflicts with your edits as inline markers in the PR: fix them there before merging (brigade:lint fails until then). On GitHub, the token also needs the Workflows permission, since updates change workflow files.

The pins in brigade's own files (.miserc.toml, .brigade/, its workflows, .gitlab-ci.yml) come with these updates: Renovate leaves them alone, since a change there would fail brigade:lint. Your own files (package.json, mise.toml, your workflows...) are updated with dependencies.

Renovate reads this from brigade's config (.brigade/configs/renovate.json): your Renovate config can still change the PR, for example its commit type with a packageRules entry on matchDepNames: ["brigade"]. If it sets includePaths, add .brigade/copier/answers.yml. Keep brigade out of groups (such as group:all): Copier needs a clean tree, so the update must be its own PR.

To update every day and merge automatically once the checks pass, answer operate_schedule: "0 5 * * *" and renovate_automerge: true, and make your checks required (GitHub: a branch ruleset, and "Allow auto-merge" in Settings). A failing check, or Copier's conflict markers in a brigade update, keep the PR open.

items.title: Ansible
items.text:
ansible installs ansible-core and runs your playbooks on your inventory: playbooks/deploy.yml in the deploy stage (after publish, and manual runs), playbooks/operate.yml in the operate stage (manual runs and operate_schedule), both with -i inventory. Other paths or options: change the commands (ansible_deploy_command, ansible_operate_command), or add ansible.cfg.

In CI, two optional secrets (CI/CD variables on GitLab, of type Variable):

  • ANSIBLE_PRIVATE_KEY: the SSH private key. Ansible loads it into an SSH agent of its own (ANSIBLE_SSH_AGENT=auto, ansible-core 2.19 or later), with no key file. Without it, the tasks keep your own SSH setup. On GitLab, brigade's image has no SSH client yet (#139).
  • ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD: the vault password. When it is set, the tasks add --vault-password-file .brigade/scripts/ansible_vault_password.py, a script that prints it. Without it, Ansible uses your own setup (ansible.cfg, ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE), so it works the same locally: ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD=... mise run deploy.

Lint the playbooks with ansible-lint, test roles with molecule.

items.title: Toolchain
items.text: Create the project with uv init: uv is always installed, and picks Python from .python-version and requires-python.

items.title: Molecule
items.text:
molecule:test runs every scenario of molecule/ (molecule test --all), with the Docker driver of molecule-plugins and ansible-core installed alongside. molecule init scenario writes a scenario to fill in; for Docker, set the driver and an image with Python (pre_build_image uses it as is; without it, the driver builds an image and needs rsync):

# molecule/default/molecule.yml
driver:
  name: docker
platforms:
  - name: instance
    image: docker.io/library/python:3.13-slim
    pre_build_image: true

The other tasks stay out of the pipeline and work on the default scenario. Arguments go to the command: mise run molecule:converge -- -s <scenario>; molecule:reconverge passes them to converge only (its molecule:destroy takes the default scenario). The tasks run Molecule with mise exec pipx:molecule@<version>, so that its ansible-playbook (with the Docker libraries) comes before the ansible tool's.

It needs Docker, also in CI: GitHub runners and act have it; on GitLab and Gitea, the runner must give the job access to a Docker daemon (mounted socket or DOCKER_HOST).

items.title: Run the CI locally
items.text:
Pick act (GitHub, Gitea, Forgejo) or gitlab-ci-local (GitLab): act:test or gitlab-ci-local:test replays the CI of pull requests in Docker, as part of the test stage.

  • It needs Docker, also in CI: GitHub runners have it; on GitLab, the task does nothing in a pipeline, and on Gitea it depends on the runner.
  • Inside the replayed CI, its test job runs the task again: there it does nothing (act sets ACT, gitlab-ci-local sets GITLAB_CI), so the replay does not loop.
  • In CI, the test job then replays the whole CI once more, which takes longer.
  • Parallel replayed jobs share the remote actions: act runs with --use-new-action-cache, so a job never copies an action another one is rewriting.

items.title: Customize a version or a command
items.text:
Each tool has one file with its version and its commands. Answer yes to customize_tools and Copier asks, for each selected tool, a version, a config file (tools with one in .brigade/configs/) and a command:

Customize tool versions and commands? (y/N) y
ruff version (empty for brigade's):
Config file of ruff, from the project root (empty for brigade's): ruff.toml
Command of ruff:lint (empty for brigade's): ruff check src
  • An answer replaces brigade's value, and stays on brigade:update until you change it.
  • An empty answer takes brigade's value, and keeps following it on brigade:update. Clear an answer to go back to it.

Answers are named <tool>_version, <tool>_config and <tool>_<action>_command, e.g. ruff_version, ruff_config, zensical_serve_command. To change them later, see Questions.

Missing a tool? Add your own task: see Custom tasks.

items.title: Updating
items.text:
Fresh deliveries: a new brigade release, straight to your kitchen.

mise run brigade:update

This runs copier update with the answers in .brigade/copier/answers.yml (edited in .brigade/copier/data.yml, see Changing answers) and applies the latest brigade release: new tool versions, new tasks, CI changes. Commit your work first: Copier needs a clean git tree, and shows conflicts as inline markers.

mise run brigade:update --help lists its options: --vcs-ref X.Y.Z updates to that version instead of the latest, --defaults takes the default of each new question instead of asking it, and Copier's other copier update options follow (mise run brigade:update --pretend).

With the renovate tool, Renovate opens this update as a PR on each release (see brigade updates); with the brigade tool, brigade:lint tells when a release is out.

brigade releases are tagged X.Y.Z. Tool versions are bumped by Renovate in brigade, so a project gets them through a release and brigade:update.

items.title: Lockfile
items.text:
.brigade/mise.lock holds the exact version of each brigade tool, with the URL and checksum of its download for Linux, macOS and Windows; .brigade/.mise/locks/ holds the Python and npm dependencies of the pipx: and npm: tools. brigade:update writes them after each update (mise -C .brigade install, then mise -C .brigade lock; from the root, mise lock only locks your mise.toml when you have one): commit them with it. The install comes first because mise lock leaves out what only an install records (an npm package's provenance): CI's install would add it, and the modified lockfile would make deno publish or GoReleaser refuse to release. Then mise install, locally and in CI, installs these versions and fails when a download does not match its checksum (a release republished under the same version). Without a lockfile, it installs the pinned versions without checksums.

A failed install or lock (offline...) does not fail the update: run mise -C .brigade install and mise -C .brigade lock again. The tools you add in your mise.toml are locked with mise lock, in your own mise.lock next to it.

items.title: What is overwritten
items.text:
Files generated by brigade belong to brigade: local edits show up as conflicts on update. The brigade tool (brigade:lint) catches them before: see brigade.

Files you add are yours: brigade never touches them, such as mise.toml, your own workflows or .gitlab/ci/*.yml files.

See CI platforms. For your own tasks, see Custom tasks.

items.title: From brigade 0.33 and earlier
items.text: Since 0.34, .brigade/configs/ls-lint.yml is brigade's, with naming rules per language (see Tool configs), instead of a starting point with no rules. If you wrote your own rules in it, move them to your own file first, set ls_lint_config to it in .brigade/copier/data.yml, then run mise run brigade:update. Otherwise, the update brings brigade's rules: fix the names ls-lint:lint reports, or keep your own file as above.

items.title: From brigade 0.28 and earlier
items.text:
Since 0.29, Renovate reads .brigade/configs/renovate.json and, by default, only updates brigade (see operate):

  • To keep your dependencies updated, add dependencies to renovate_updates in .brigade/copier/data.yml.
  • The renovate.json of Renovate's onboarding PR is no longer needed: delete it, unless it holds your own settings.

items.title: From brigade 0.27 and earlier
items.text:
Since 0.28, releasaurus reads .brigade/configs/releasaurus.toml (see release):

  • A releasaurus.toml at the root is no longer read: move it (e.g. to .github/releasaurus.toml), add tag_prefix = "" to a [[package]] with path = ".", and set releasaurus_config to it in .brigade/copier/data.yml.
  • Only feat, fix, perf, revert and breaking changes make a release.
  • The release pull request also updates your manifests (package.json, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml...): a version left at 0.0.0 jumps to the next release's.

items.title: From brigade 0.25 and earlier
items.text: Since 0.26, git hooks come from the prek tool: brigade:hooks and brigade:pre-commit are gone. A hook installed with brigade:hooks calls mise run brigade:pre-commit, so each commit fails after the update: delete .git/hooks/pre-commit, or select prek (tools in .brigade/copier/data.yml), run mise run brigade:update, then mise run prek:install (it replaces the old hook).

items.title: From brigade 0.24 and earlier
items.text: Since 0.25, the tool configs in .brigade/configs/ hold brigade's settings and belong to brigade, except goreleaser, container-structure-test, ls-lint and sqlfluff, which stay yours (see Tool configs). brigade:update merges brigade's changes into them; then brigade:lint shows the ones you had edited as edited. For each: move your settings to your own file (e.g. ruff.toml at the root), set <tool>_config to it in .brigade/copier/data.yml, and run mise run brigade:update, which restores brigade's file.

items.title: From brigade 0.23 and earlier
items.text:
Since 0.24, the tool files are in .brigade/conf.d/ (was .brigade/tools/), so that mise writes one lockfile for them all. Update as usual: Copier moves them. This first update runs the previous brigade:update, which does not lock: then run mise -C .brigade install and mise -C .brigade lock (mise may ask you to trust the moved files: mise trust), and commit the update with .brigade/mise.lock and .brigade/.mise/.

.brigade/.mise/locks/ holds the tools' locked dependencies (uv.lock, aube-lock.yaml, package.json). Until 0.25, the tool configs in .brigade/configs/ were yours, so not updated: exclude it in the ones you have, as new projects do (0.25 does it for brigade's configs):

  • yamllint.yml: .mise/ in ignore;
  • trivy.yaml: "**/.mise" in scan.skip-dirs;
  • ansible-lint.yml: "**/.mise" in exclude_paths;
  • biome-brigade.jsonc: "!**/.mise" in files.includes.

items.title: From brigade 0.12 and earlier
items.text:
Since 0.13, the answers are in .brigade/copier/. Update as usual (or merge Renovate's PR), then move them:

mise run brigade:update
git mv .brigade/answers.yml .brigade/copier/answers.yml
git commit -m "chore: move brigade answers"

Until then, brigade:lint fails and brigade:update cannot find the answers.

items.title: From brigade 0.5 and earlier
items.text:
Before 0.6, brigade's files were in .mise/ and .github/actions/ (.gitea/actions/, .gitlab/ci/). Move your answers, then update:

mkdir -p .brigade/copier
git mv .mise/brigade-copier-answers.yml .brigade/copier/answers.yml
git commit -m "chore: move brigade answers"
uvx copier@9.19.1 update -a .brigade/copier/answers.yml

Copier removes the old generated files. Move your own files out of .mise/ into mise.toml (see Custom tasks): mise no longer reads .mise/.
